summary: Describes common misinterpretations and ambiguities in Signaling Compression (SigComp), a scheme for compressing messages from protocols such as SIP, and gives developers guidance. It updates RFC 3320, RFC 3321, and RFC 3485. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Some rules for squeezing messages smaller were confusing. This note clears up the confusing parts so everyone squeezes and unsqueezes the same way.

questions: what is sigcomp decompression memory size
what are the sigcomp static dictionary bugs
subtitle: Fixes and clarifications for places where SigComp implementers read the original specs differently.

tldr.problem: SigComp specifies the decompressor in great detail but leaves the compressor to the implementer. Interoperability testing exposed ambiguities and misreadings in RFC 3320, RFC 3321 and RFC 3485.
tldr.mechanism: The document goes through each problem area, such as memory sizing, byte copying, state retention priority, feedback and the static dictionary, and states the intended behavior.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 3320, RFC 3321 and RFC 3485 without changing the SigComp version, so implementers get one agreed reading of the unclear parts.

today: RFC 4896 is a Proposed Standard from June 2007 that updates RFC 3320, RFC 3321 and RFC 3485. Its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why SigComp Needed Clarifying
sections.content:
SigComp (RFC 3320) defines the Universal Decompressor Virtual Machine (UDVM) that decompresses messages from a compliant compressor. It also covers state handling and message structure. The decompressor's behavior is specified in great detail, but the compressor's is left to the implementer.

During implementation and interoperability tests, several areas turned out to need clarification. This document lists them. It cites the original text as, for example, "RFC 3320-Section 3.4" to separate it from its own sections.
sections.eli5: Imagine a game whose rules for one player were written very carefully and the rules for the other player were left vague. People started to disagree, so someone wrote a note to settle it.

sections.title: Memory Size and Byte Copying
sections.content:
The default Decompression Memory Size (DMS) is 2K. When a message carries bytecode, as the first one will, two copies of the bytecode sit in decompressor memory. That is correct, but the text points out that bytecode of three to four hundred bytes then seriously restricts the circular buffer and the message. Applications that mandate SigComp are told to also mandate an appropriately sized DMS, and a worked example arrives at 8k.

The byte copying rules of RFC 3320 were misleading. Copying bytes outside the bounds set by byte_copy_left and byte_copy_right is legitimate. Those two values only define a circular buffer, and a copy that reaches the right bound wraps back to the left bound. If byte_copy_right is less than byte_copy_left, reads and writes skip the memory between them.

The byte copying rules also apply when state is created from STATE-CREATE or END-MESSAGE, and to CRC. They do not apply when reading feedback items.
sections.eli5: The machine has a small notebook to work in. If the instructions take up too much of the notebook, there is little room left, so you need a bigger notebook. The notebook also wraps around, like writing in a circle.

sections.title: UDVM Instruction Details
sections.content:
If INPUT-BYTES or INPUT-BITS asks for more data than is left in the message, the dispatcher MUST NOT return any of it, and the bytes that remain MUST stay unchanged. The program jumps to the address given. A partial byte left by INPUT-BITS is still thrown away, and INPUT-BYTES (0, a, b) can flush it.

MULTILOAD must behave as if executed step by step, so it cannot write over its own opcode or parameters, and any indirection is resolved at execution time. STATE-FREE does not check the minimum access length, because state cannot be freed until the application authenticates the message, and it only affects state in the current compartment.

If the stack fill value is 0xFFFF when a push happens, the fill value MUST wrap to 0x0000 and be written back, which overwrites the pushed value.
sections.eli5: If a recipe says to take six eggs and only three are left, you take none and move to the next step. The little rules here make sure every cook does exactly the same thing.

sections.title: State, Priorities and Identifier Clashes
sections.content:
For state_retention_priority the order is 65535 < 0 < 1 < ... < 65534, so 65535 is the lowest. Retention priority MUST belong to the compartment, not the piece of state. The same state created with a different priority is stored once, counts once against the state memory size (SMS), and just has its priority updated. Creating state that already exists SHOULD refresh its creation time.

Minimum priority state (65535) can be created at a decompressor without the remote compressor knowing. With more than one such item, the compressor cannot be sure which is still present, and the examples show decompression failures. Where NACK is unsupported, the recommendation is that only one piece of minimum priority state SHOULD be present in a compartment. If both ends support NACK, this MAY be relaxed.

State is created using the full 20-byte hash, but accessed with only the first n bytes, where n may be as low as 6. Using the birthday paradox with a 6-octet identifier, the clash chance is 0.018% at 1,000,000 states and 16.28% at 10,000,000. With the full 20 octets it is vanishingly small.
sections.eli5: It is like a coat check where tickets only show the first few letters of a name. With a few coats that works fine, but with millions of coats two tickets may look the same, so use longer tickets.

sections.title: Feedback and Advertising Resources
sections.content:
An endpoint SHOULD return requested feedback even if its SMS is zero, and the feedback storage is not part of the SMS. It SHOULD keep sending feedback until a valid message updates it. If requested_feedback_location is zero, existing feedback is left untouched. If it is nonzero but the Q flag is zero, existing feedback SHOULD be overwritten with "no feedback data".

The I-bit tells the remote endpoint that the sender will not access its locally available state, so the endpoint may skip advertising it and reclaim that memory. It still SHOULD advertise parameters such as DMS and SMS. The compressor MUST NOT use more resources than the most recently advertised. Reducing resources SHOULD NOT be done unless absolutely necessary, and memory MUST NOT be reclaimed until the other end acknowledges the advertisement.

Locally available state, such as dictionaries, is not fully defined by SigComp, so without further definition it SHOULD NOT be used. The shared mode of RFC 3321 is well defined, with state mapped into the compartment at minimum priority.
sections.eli5: The two sides keep telling each other how much room they have. They should not use more room than the last thing they were told, and should only shrink the room after the other side says it heard.

sections.title: Uncompressed Bytecode and the Static Dictionary
sections.content:
It is possible to write bytecode that simply outputs the whole message, effectively sending it uncompressed inside a SigComp message. This is useful when the bytecode is well known, since a decompressor can recognize it and output the bytes without running a VM. The RFC gives its mnemonic code and the resulting 13-byte SigComp message.

The SIP/SDP static dictionary of RFC 3485 has five prioritized sections, and its offset table has some minor bugs. Five strings (application, sdp, send, recv and phone) are listed in the offset table under a priority section that does not contain them. The RFC does not fix the dictionary, because the change would break backward compatibility. It tells implementers to avoid those offsets unless the matching string section was loaded.
sections.eli5: A dictionary has a few wrong page numbers. Rather than reprint every copy, the note tells you which entries to skip.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says that its updates do not change the security considerations of SigComp. It goes over the known risks: snooping into other users' state, faking state, using SigComp in a DoS attack, filling state to attack SigComp, and looping code in the UDVM.

Each is already limited. Snooping is mitigated by using at least 48 bits of the hash, a minimum this update does not reduce. Application-layer authorization guards state changes. SigComp produces only one decompressed message per compressed one, and the UDVM cycle limit stops looping code. The IANA section says no versions change, so the IANA considerations stay the same.
sections.eli5: The safety rules stay as they were. This note only makes the rules easier to follow.
